'''Orleans Parish Prison''' is the city [[jail]] for [[New Orleans]], Louisiana.  First opened in 1837, it is operated by the [[Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office (Louisiana)|Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office]]. Most of the prisoners—1,300 of the 1,500 or so as of June 2016—are awaiting trial.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://data.nola.gov/City-Administration/Number-of-pre-trial-detainees-in-Orleans-Parish-Pr/fnsq-kszc |title=Number of pre-trial detainees in Orleans Parish Prison (1007) |website=City of New Orleans Open Data |date=2016-06-30 |accessdate=2016-11-22}}</ref>

In May 2013, Orleans Parish Prison ranked as one of the ten worst prisons in the United States, based on reporting in ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]'' magazine.<ref>{{cite web|author1=James Ridgeway|author2=Jean Casella|title=America's 10 Worst Prisons: NOLA|url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2013/05/10-worst-prisons-america-orleans-parish-opp|website=Mother Jones|accessdate=2016-11-30|date=2013-05-06}}</ref>
==Early history==

=== First location ===
[[File:Police Jail & Parish Prison, New Orleans, 1864.png|left|thumb|The first Orleans Parish Prison in 1864]]
The old Parish Prison opened in 1837 on the square bound by Orleans, [[Tremé]], St. Ann, and Marais.<ref name=":0" /> Architects Joseph Pilié and A. Voilquin designed it in an austere Franco-Spanish style with two cupolas, and it was built during 1831–1836. It was progressively organized, with sections for different offenders and offenses.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Campanella|first=Richard|date=April 2016|title=Ominous: New Orleans’ Old Criminal Courts Building and a Brief History of Penal Architecture|url=https://richcampanella.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/article_Campanella_Preservation-in-Print_2016_April_Criminal-Courts-Building.pdf|access-date=2026-05-12|website=Preservation in Print}}</ref>

During the day, prisoners were kept outside in the segregated courtyards. At night, most prisoners slept on the floor of crowded cells with only two blankets each.<ref name=":0" />

In 1895, ''[[The Times-Picayune]]'' described Orleans Parish Prison as:

{{quote|"the place where refractory slaves were sent to receive a dose of cat o'nine tails, or to be confined in the dungeons in extreme cases the rebellious blacks were kept dark cells on a diet of bread and water. Jailors subjected enslaved people to degrading and torturous prison conditions as a punishment for running away."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://neworleanshistorical.org/items/show/929 | title="Confined in the Dungeons": Orleans Parish Prison and Self-Emancipated People }}</ref>}}

In 1891, an angry mob [[1891 New Orleans lynchings|breached the prison and lynched 11 Italian men]] who had been acquitted of the murder of Police Chief [[David Hennessy|David C. Hennessy]], hastening plans to replace the prison.<ref name=":02" /> The prison closed in early 1895. The location was later used to construct a building for the Sewerage and Water Board that is today just behind [[Municipal Auditorium (New Orleans)|Municipal Auditorium]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Second location ===
[[File:Elk Place Courthouse New Orleans 1900.png|left|thumb|The second Orleans Parish Prison at left, next to the contemporary [[Orleans Parish Criminal Courts Building#Elk Place courthouse|Criminal Courts Building]], around 1900]]
The new parish prison was behind the [[Orleans Parish Criminal Courts Building#Elk Place courthouse|Criminal Courts Building at Elks Place]] on Tulane and Saratoga.<ref name=":0" /> It was designed by Max A. Orlopp Jr., who specialized in [[Richardsonian Romanesque|Richardson Romanesque]] courthouses in Southern cities. The location was considered at the time to be a tough neighborhood, and the large judicial, police, and prison complex was intended to convey judicial power and order.<ref name=":02" />
{{Clear left}}

=== Third location ===
[[File:Old Orleans Parish House of Detention.png|thumb|The third Orleans Parish Prison, in operation 1901–1929]]
[[File:Panorama Lakewards from Falstaff NOLA (cropped).jpg|thumb|Rear of the current [[Orleans Parish Criminal Courts Building]], showing its original prison facilities in 2012]]
The House of Detention on Tulane Avenue and Broad Street opened in 1901, which had formerly been the site of the second [[United States Marine Hospital (New Orleans)#Second hospital|New Orleans U.S. Marine Hospital]]. The prison was demolished in 1929 to construct the current [[Orleans Parish Criminal Courts Building]], which had its own prison facilities at its rear.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Huber |first=Leonard Victor |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/New_Orleans/3Mw4nQMvDWoC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=orleans+parish+prison+1895+1931&pg=PA284&printsec=frontcover |title=New Orleans: A Pictorial History |date=1971 |publisher=Pelican Publishing |isbn=978-1-4556-0931-4 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson, Jr.|first=Samuel|date=1982-08-10|title=Criminal Courts Building: National Register of Historic Places Nomination Form|url=https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/1f0a4887-d98f-4268-80c1-c05f07098c8d#page=4|access-date=2026-05-04|page=4}}</ref> In 1931, prison and court functions were relocated to these new facilities at Tulane and Broad.

== House of Detention and Community Corrections Center ==
[[File:Orleans Parish Prison, New Orleans July 2021.jpg|thumb|The 1967 House of Detention photographed in 2021 after its closure|left]]
In 1967, the House of Detention complex opened at 2735 Perdido St, followed by the Community Corrections Center (CCC) complex across the street in 1976.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Bernard |date=2025-06-20 |title=The towering legacy of the House of Detention |url=https://thelensnola.org/2025/06/20/the-house-of-detention-is-a-10-story-former-jail-in-new-orleans-known-for-its-poor-conditions/ |access-date=2026-05-07 |website=The Lens |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Mackel |first=Travers |date=2024-05-08 |title=As old criminal justice buildings deteriorate, concerns loom over potential NOPD move |url=https://www.wdsu.com/article/new-orleans-abandoned-criminal-justice-building-investigation/60637878 |access-date=2026-05-07 |website=WDSU |language=en}}</ref>

The Orleans Parish Prison has had tremendous problems for a long time, mostly caused by lack of monitoring of the inmates by [[sheriffs in the United States#Sheriff's offices|deputies]]. Several fights, stabbings and deaths have occurred in the prison, mostly in the 13-story high-rise House of Detention which has become infamous.   
A group of inmates filed a class-action lawsuit against the jail in 1969 but problems still went unaddressed. Statistics researchers considered Orleans Parish Prison to be probably the worst jail in the country. The prison was described as too large, understaffed, and filthy. Prisoners lived in fear of being beaten or raped. In 2012 there were 600 ambulance runs to the emergency room, with more than half of them related to violence.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://portside.org/2014-04-03/dont-expect-safe-humane-orleans-parish-prison-any-time-soon-heres-why | title=Don't Expect a Safe, Humane Orleans Parish Prison Any Time Soon; Here's Why | date=3 April 2014 }}</ref> Guards rarely patrolled the House of Detention, one of several buildings comprising the Orleans Parish Prison complex. Prisoners had access to drugs and weapons such as kitchen knives and handguns by way of guards.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://neworleanscitybusiness.com/blog/2011/11/17/opp-guards-inmate-detail-brutality-inside-jail/ | title=Prison guards, inmate detail brutality inside jail &#124; New Orleans CityBusiness | date=17 November 2011 }}</ref>

=== Abandonment during Hurricane Katrina ===
On August 29, 2005, when [[Hurricane Katrina]]–an extremely destructive and deadly category 5 hurricane–struck the Gulf Coast, the staff of [[Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office (Louisiana)|Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office]] abandoned the jail, leaving roughly 650 prisoners in their cells with no access to food, water, or ventilation for days.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2005/09/21/new-orleans-prisoners-abandoned-floodwaters|title=New Orleans: Prisoners Abandoned to Floodwaters|date=2005-09-21|work=Human Rights Watch|access-date=2018-09-12|language=en}}</ref> Deputies returned to the Orleans Parish Prison days later and began evacuating inmates to surrounding areas which included the [[Elayn Hunt Correctional Center]], the [[Interstate 10|I-10]] overpass, and the Broad Avenue overpass.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/hurricane-katrina-was-a-nightmare-for-inmates-in-new-orleans-829/|title=Hurricane Katrina Was a Nightmare for Inmates in New Orleans|date=2015-08-29|work=Vice|access-date=2018-09-12|language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aclu.org/news/aclu-report-details-horrors-suffered-orleans-parish-prisoners-wake-hurricane-katrina|title=ACLU Report Details Horrors Suffered by Orleans Parish Prisoners in Wake of Hurricane Katrina|work=American Civil Liberties Union|access-date=2018-09-12|language=en}}</ref>

In over 400 testimonials conducted by the [[American Civil Liberties Union]], prisoners described their experiences during the abandonment which included exposure to floodwater and other elements, hunger, beatings by jail staff and other inmates, and other racially-charged abuse by jail staff.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.aclu.org/other/summaries-400-testimonials-inmates-incarcerated-orleans-parish-prison-during-hurricane-katrina|title=Summaries of 400 Testimonials From Inmates Incarcerated at Orleans Parish Prison During Hurricane Katrina|work=American Civil Liberties Union|access-date=2018-09-12|language=en}}</ref> While there is no official death count for prisoners that were left behind, 517 prisoners were later registered as "unaccounted for" by [[Human Rights Watch|Humans Rights Watch]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2005/10/katr-o01.html|title=New Orleans prisoners left to drown after Katrina struck|last=Michaels|first=Fergus|access-date=2018-09-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thesocietypages.org/socimages/2011/08/27/imprisoned-disaster-political-will-and-hurricane-katrina/|title=The Fate of Prisoners during Hurricane Katrina - Sociological Images |work=The Society Pages |language=en|access-date=2018-09-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.alternet.org/story/26073/left_to_die_in_a_new_orleans_prison|title=Left to Die in a New Orleans Prison|last=Goodman|first=Amy|date=2005-09-27|work=AlterNet|access-date=2018-09-12}}</ref>

CCC has since been abandoned since 2005, and HOD closed in 2012.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

Between April 2006 and April 2014, ''[[The Times-Picayune]]'' reports 44 inmate deaths,<ref>{{cite web|author=Naomi Martin and Richard A. Webster|url=http://www.nola.com/crime/index.ssf/2014/10/opp_inmate_deaths_since_hurric.html|title=Dying at OPP: 44 inmates dead in 9 years|website=NOLA.com|date=2014-10-07|accessdate=2016-11-28
}}</ref> including seven "uncounted" deaths,<ref>{{cite web|author=Naomi Martin|url=http://www.nola.com/articles/14180428/deaths_go_uncounted_at_orleans.amp|title=Inmate deaths sometimes go uncounted at Orleans Parish Prison|website=NOLA.com|date=2014-10-14|accessdate=2016-11-28}}</ref> referring to inmates released shortly before their deaths. Since the report, there have been five additional fatalities,<ref>{{cite web|author=Adina Marx-Arpadi|url=https://opprcnola.org/the-context/timeline-of-deaths-in-opp/|title=DEATHS IN OPP ~ 2009 to present|website=Orleans Parish Prison Reform Coalition|date=2016-10-28|accessdate=2016-11-28}}</ref> bringing the total to 49 since April 2006.

== Current facility ==
[[File:Orleans Parish Prison from I-10, New Orleans, 25th November 2019 04.jpg|thumb|The current prison facility in 2019]]
The [[Federal Emergency Management Agency]] dedicated $223 million to the Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office for restoration of its facilities following [[Hurricane Katrina]] in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fema.gov/news-release/2011/07/01/fema-funds-new-admin-building-orleans-criminal-sheriffs-office|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161114182316/https://www.fema.gov/news-release/2011/07/01/fema-funds-new-admin-building-orleans-criminal-sheriffs-office|url-status=dead|archive-date=14 November 2016|publisher=[[Federal Emergency Management Agency]]|title=FEMA Funds New Admin Building for Orleans Criminal Sheriff's Office|website=FEMA.gov|date=2012-07-16|accessdate=2016-11-26}}</ref> The Sheriff's Office has outlined three phases of construction that would utilize these funds.

The Phase I facility is a three-story, {{convert|163,885|sqfoot|m2}} building consisting of a kitchen and warehouse.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.opso.us/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=237:orleans-parish-sheriffs-office-breaks-ground-on-new-kitchenwarehouse-facility&catid=1:latest-news |title=Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office Breaks Ground on New Kitchen/Warehouse Facility |website=Orleans Parish Sheriff’s Office |date=2010-03-02 |accessdate=2016-11-26}}</ref> Opened in 2015,<ref>{{cite web|author=Kelsey Davis |url=http://www.wdsu.com/article/orleans-parish-sheriff-s-office-completes-inmate-transfer-to-new-facility/3379835 |title=Orleans Parish Sheriff's Office completes inmate transfer to new facility |website=WDSU News |date=2015-09-15 |accessdate=2016-11-15}}</ref> Phase II contains 1,438 beds and cost $146 million to construct.<ref name="nola-opening">{{cite web|author=Jonathan Bullington |url=http://www.nola.com/crime/index.ssf/2015/09/orleans_parish_jail_opens.html |title=First inmates arrive at Orleans Parish new jail facility |website=NOLA.com |date=2015-09-14 |accessdate=2016-11-15}}</ref>

The Sheriff’s Office plans to build an additional 750-bed facility as Phase III.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nolacitycouncil.com/content/display.asp?id=54&nid=%7BB812C65F-9A59-42AB-A122-3AC8465421E8%7D |title=Criminal Justice Committee to Hold Special Meeting to Address Issues Surrounding Orleans Parish Prison |website=New Orleans City Council |date=2015-07-06 |accessdate=2016-11-26}}</ref> The Orleans Parish Prison Reform Coalition opposes the plan,<ref>{{cite web |author=Laura McKnight |url=http://www.nola.com/crime/index.ssf/2016/11/group_opposed_to_jail_expansio.html |title=Group opposed to jail expansion invites officials, public to meeting |website=NOLA.com |date=2016-11-16 |accessdate=2016-11-26}}</ref> calling on former Democratic Mayor [[Mitch Landrieu]]'s office to "oppose any options involving the expansion of the jail," and instead support "retrofitting of the current jail to better care for incarcerated special populations."<ref>{{cite web|author=Adina Marx-Arpadi|url=https://opprcnola.org/2016/11/16/open-letter-to-mayor-landrieu-re-opposition-to-jail-expansion/|title=Open Letter to Mayor Landrieu re: Opposition to Jail Expansion|website=Orleans Parish Prison Reform Coalition|date=2016-11-16|accessdate=2016-11-26}}</ref> In 2021, [[Susan Hutson]] defeated longtime incumbent [[Marlin N. Gusman]] to become the city's next sheriff.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Susan Hutson defeats long-time Orleans Parish Sheriff Marlin Gusman |url=https://www.wwltv.com/article/news/local/orleans/susan-hutson-defeats-long-time-sheriff-marlin-gusman-wwl-tv-projection/289-e28ee76c-dede-4096-8add-297f0b7a0701|access-date=12 April 2024|work=WWL|date=11 December 2021 }}</ref> Her campaign was centered on opposition to the Phase III planned jail expansion.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The first female sheriff of Orleans Parish is also the first Black woman to hold the job in Louisiana|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/12/12/us/first-female-black-sheriff-orleans-parish/index.html|access-date=12 April 2024|work=CNN|date=12 December 2021 }}</ref> Nonetheless, it was ultimately unsuccessful; in 2023, a federal judge ordered the city to begin construction.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sheriff Hutson's opposition to Orleans jail expansion has 'reached finish line,' federal judge says|url=https://www.fox8live.com/2023/09/05/sheriff-hutsons-opposition-orleans-jail-expansion-has-reached-finish-line-federal-judge-says/|access-date=17 April 2024|work=Fox 8|date=5 September 2023 }}</ref>

Just after midnight on May 16, 2025, ten inmates (including six charged with murder or attempted murder) [[2025 New Orleans jailbreak|escaped]] from Orleans Parish Prison through a hole behind a toilet; eight of the ten would be recaptured by May 26. One of the two final inmates at large, Antoine Massey, would be recaptured on June 27, 2025. The final escapee, Derrick Groves, was recaptured on October 8, 2025, nearly five months after the jailbreak.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-10-08 |title=Last of the 10 New Orleans jail escapees from May is captured in Georgia, authorities say |url=https://abc7ny.com/post/last-10-new-orleans-jail-escapees-may-is-captured-georgia-authorities-say/17965438/ |access-date=2025-10-12 |website=ABC7 New York |language=en}}</ref>

==Notable inmates==
The 10 to 12 adult women onboard the ''[[Golden Venture]]'' vessel from China that washed ashore in the [[Rockaways]] in [[New York City]] in June 1993 were kept at Orleans Parish Prison for a few years.<ref>Law, Victoria, "Recommended Reading: Reports," ''Resistance Behind Bars: The Struggles of Incarcerated Women'' (Oakland, CA: PM Press, 2009), p. 198</ref>

On November 29, 2015, [[Louisiana State Senate|state Senator]] [[Troy E. Brown]] of [[Ascension Parish, Louisiana|Ascension Parish]] was booked in the Orleans Parish Prison for [[Domestic violence|domestic abuse battery]], a [[misdemeanor]] stemming from an incident with his alleged long-term paramour, a woman from [[Labadieville, Louisiana|Labadieville]], at the [[Hyatt|Hyatt Regency Hotel]] near the [[Caesars Superdome|Superdome]] in New Orleans.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://theadvocate.com/news/14143572-123/police-state-sen-troy-brown|title=Police: State Sen. Troy Brown arrested, accused of punching girlfriend in face Saturday night at New Orleans hotel|newspaper=[[The Advocate (Louisiana)|The Baton Rouge Advocate]]|author=David J. Mitchell and Jim Mustian|accessdate=November 30, 2015}}</ref>
